rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alif Lām Rā serves as the sūrah’s identifying name; the same name appears for Yūnus and Hūd, and its meaning need not be pursued.
rows.anchor: Alif Lām Rā is the Qur’ ānic name of the sūrah. Sūrahs Yūnus and H ūd also have the same name.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrahs sharing names share meanings and topics; these three sūrahs have the same underlying topic.
rows.anchor: Hence the real topic in each of these three sūrahs is the same;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the three sūrahs share a topic, their discussions and reasoning differ.
rows.anchor: discussion and reasoning is different.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book is lucid in its statements and arguments, offers indisputable proofs, and uses an effective style that removes doubts.
rows.anchor: This book is absolutely clear and lucid in what it states and the argument it provides; everything it presents is evident through indisputable proofs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’ān itself contains decisive proofs, so it needs no external miracle; people need only listen and reflect.
rows.anchor: arguments as radiant as the sun are found within it that testify to its veracity. The only thing needed is that people open their ears to hear it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address favors Arabia generally and Quraysh particularly by revealing the Book in their language; they should understand, value, convey, and explain it, which is one sense of its clarity.
rows.anchor: The verse addresses the people of Arabia in general and the Quraysh in particular and expresses the favour God has done to them by revealing His book in their own language

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh are warned that neglecting this great boon will make them especially unfortunate and bring punishment.
rows.anchor: Concealed in this word is also a warning for the Quraysh that if they do not duly value it, they will be the most unfortunate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qaṣaṣ means stories or anecdotes, not the act or style of narrating; the grammatical construction and article alif-lām support this reading.
rows.anchor: means “story, tale and anecdote” and is not used as a participle to mean “narrating [something].” If it was used in this meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’ānic parallels support reading qaṣaṣ as an anecdote rather than a narrative style.
rows.anchor: Parallels from the Qur’ān corroborate this. Thus, for example, verse 176 of Sūrah al-A‘rāf says:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He equates ‘best stories’ with the Qur’ān’s phrase ‘best discourse’ in 39:23.
rows.anchor: is the same as the one found in verse 23 of S ūrah al-Zumar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Treating qaṣaṣ as a participle would remove its grammatical object, although the verb requires one and is consistently used with an object in the Qur’ān.
rows.anchor: if the word !!ﻗﺼﺺ is understood as a participle, the grammatical object (maf‘ūl) disappears; whereas a verb requires an object

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse shifts from a general warning to Quraysh to direct address of the Prophet and presents the anecdote as both excellent and evidence of his messengership.
rows.anchor: Deliberation shows that there are two important aspects of this anecdote

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A true story that mirrors its audience’s life is especially effective; Joseph’s story reflects the Prophet’s present and future, including severe trials and a bright outcome.
rows.anchor: If an anecdote is true in itself and also acts as a mirror to its addressees in which they can see the ups and downs of their lives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story foreshadows the Prophet’s path from the cave of Thawr to political ascendancy in Madīnah and the eventual submission of arrogant Makkans.
rows.anchor: from the darkness of this cave the radiance of obtaining the political ascendancy in Madīnah could also be observed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s lack of literacy and prior access to religious scriptures makes this detailed, true account evidence of revelation and his messengership to both his people and the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: he was neither aware of this anecdote nor had any means of being aware of it. It was because of the Qur’ ān that he became cognizant of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ‘before this’ implies the Prophet had not known the story earlier; if he had, he would have mentioned it during his forty years.
rows.anchor: if he had known it to any extent before the revelation of the Qur’ ān, he would have referred to it one time or the other in the forty years of his existence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the story occurs in the Torah and Talmud, the Prophet had no means of learning it; the Qur’ānic account is natural and coherent, unlike those accounts, and upholds prophetic dignity.
rows.anchor: the account of the Qur’ ān is very natural and that of the Torah is illogical and unnatural and also against the majesty of the prophetic status.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s dream begins the prelude to the main anecdote.
rows.anchor: This is the beginning of the prelude to the actual anecdote.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s choice to bring the dream to his father first signals uprightness, sincere intent, and obedience; he treats it as meaningful rather than boasting about it.
rows.anchor: The fact that Joseph (sws) foremost brought this dream before his father’s attention shows his extraordinary uprightness, sincere intention and forthright obedience.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph first tells his father because he trusts him completely.
rows.anchor: presented it before his illustrious father the foremost because he fully trusted him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s humility appears in his hesitant narration: he names the heavenly bodies first, then cautiously says they prostrated; repeating ‘I saw’ signals hesitation.
rows.anchor: The repetition of the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob understands the dream to foretell Joseph’s prophethood and warns him not to tell his brothers, lest jealousy lead them to plot against him.
rows.anchor: Jacob (sws) immediately realized that this dream meant that Joseph (sws) would one day be appointed a prophet and for this reason he stopped him from narrating it before his brothers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph had eleven brothers: ten were his stepbrothers, while Benjamin was his only full brother.
rows.anchor: Joseph (sws) had eleven brothers; out of these, ten were step. Only the youngest – Benjamin – was his real brother.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob recognizes the dream as true because prophethood begins with true dreams; its apparent meaning predicts a brilliant future and imminent prophethood for Joseph.
rows.anchor: propehthood begins with such true dreams. The apparent nature of the dream showed its true nature and predicted a brilliant future

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One implication of teaching Joseph the interpretation of events is that God will reveal the reality of this dream, as its fulfillment is later described in 12:100–101.
rows.anchor: First, God himself will make evident to him the reality of this dream. Thus later in the sūrah in verses 100-101, it is said:

none: Translation of verses 12:102-111 only; no commentary point is added.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘That’ refers to the story just narrated; the Prophet learned it only through revelation, since he was absent when Joseph’s brothers conspired and decided to throw him in a well.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) had no way of knowing it. It was merely God’s grace that he came to know about it through divine revelation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was unlettered and had no access to the Torah account; differences at every step make the Qur’ānic telling more logical and closer to human nature as revelation.
rows.anchor: Any person who reflects on all these differences will be left with no option but to confess that the Qur’ ānic account is more logical and closer to the human nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s brothers held differing views while conspiring, then agreed to throw him into a well.
rows.anchor: They had different views. Finally, they agreed to throw him in a well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For people still able to accept truth, this story decisively proves the Qur’ān is from God; Quraysh and the People of the Book have lost that ability, so most will not believe despite the Prophet’s efforts.
rows.anchor: The reason for their not accepting faith is not that they have any doubt in the Qur’ān being the book of God but because their ability to accept the truth has died.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse reassures the Prophet that rejection harms the deniers, not him: he asks no payment, only delivers a reminder whose benefit or consequences belong to each hearer.
rows.anchor: The Prophet’s responsibility is to only deliver the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people’s failure to believe reflects their refusal to see and learn from the abundant signs around them, not a failure by the Prophet or Qur’ān.
rows.anchor: The real fault lies with them. They are not willing to use their eyes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This answers their demand for a sign of punishment: many signs already surround them, but they count only punishment that directly visits them as a sign.
rows.anchor: This verse actually is a rejoinder to this demand. There are several signs around them that are enough to open their eyes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many who profess belief in God also associate partners and intercessors, believing these can rescue them from God’s seizure; this belief obstructs acceptance of the Qur’ān.
rows.anchor: those among them who do believe in God, they also believe that He has many partners and intercessors.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question warns that these people will soon meet their fate if the described condition persists.
rows.anchor: This question carries a warning. If the case is what the verse points to, then soon they will meet their fate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since polytheism is the root ailment, the Prophet announces complete disavowal of it; opponents should not expect him to soften his stance.
rows.anchor: a complete acquittal from it was announced from the tongue of the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is not a polytheist and has declared his complete acquittal from shirk.
rows.anchor: polytheism and the Prophet (sws) is not a polytheist. He has declared his acquittal from it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse answers the objection that a messenger born among people should have been an angel instead.
rows.anchor: They objected that how is it possible that they accept some as God’s messenger who was born and lived among them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s final part refers to remnants of the nations of ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Madyan.
rows.anchor: The last part of the verse refers to remnants of the nations of ‘ Ād, Tham ūd and Madyan etc.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s established practice is to delay punishment until messengers have conclusively delivered truth, lose hope in their people, and the people think the warning false; then divine help comes to the messengers.
rows.anchor: First He sends His messengers who conclusively deliver the truth to people. The punishment arrives when these messengers lose hope in their nation’s accepting faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is self-explanatory and marks the close of the sūrah’s exegesis.
rows.anchor: On this self-explanatory verse ends this sūrah’s exegesis.

none: Dated colophon only; no commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like the previous sūrah, al-Kahf was revealed in the late Makkan conflict, as Quraysh sought to erase the Qur’ānic mission while Jews and Christians backed them indirectly.
rows.anchor: Like the previous sūrah, this sūrah was also revealed in that part of the Makkan period when the conflict between good and evil of the Prophet’s preaching mission had entered its final phase.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh are warned not to let worldly success lead them to reject an obvious truth, since God’s punishment is near if they persist in arrogance.
rows.anchor: The Quryash are warned that in the wake of their worldly successes they should not try to arrogantly deny an obvious reality.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet and companions are urged to patience and steadfastness, with hints of migration and glad tidings of coming victories granted by God.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) and his companions are urged to be patient and steadfast. Certain subtle indications are made of the upcoming phases of migration

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where the previous sūrah exposed Jews, al-Kahf and Maryam expose Christians; Quraysh risk losing the great opportunity God offers if they follow baseless opponents in rejecting it.
rows.anchor: Just as in the previous sūrah, S ūrah Banī Isrā’īl, the Jews are exposed, in this sūrah and in the next one – S ūrah Maryam – the Christians are exposed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s task is to warn and give glad tidings; unbelief among rebels reflects neither a defect in the Book nor a shortcoming in his preaching.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is urged to be patient since his only responsibility is to warn and give glad tidings to his nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People’s blindness comes from infatuation with worldly lures; the Prophet should not fret, because the world’s false ornament will be exposed and they will regret their conduct.
rows.anchor: The reason for this is that these people have become blind in their infatuation with the lures of this world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some insist they will not believe until they witness the punishment; a messenger’s duty is to warn and give glad tidings, while hardened hearts remain impervious to warning.
rows.anchor: They are contending that unless they are able to observe God’s punishment, they will not believe in the punishment they are being warned of by the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gives the heedless respite out of mercy and wisdom, though He could punish them immediately; the Prophet should trust God and continue patiently.
rows.anchor: His lord is gracious and merciful and for this reason giving them respite. If He wanted to immediately punish them, He could break their backs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblīs was one jinn who deceived Adam; ‘Satan’ is his title, not the name of an entire creature category, and his progeny continue his mission of leading Adam’s descendants astray.
rows.anchor: He was from among the jinnkind. He disobeyed God and was condemned. Satan is not the name of a whole category of creatures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse reminds arrogant Quraysh that Satan and his progeny are their eternal enemies.
rows.anchor: Here the arrogant among the Quraysh are reminded of the eternal enmity of Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh have made Satan and his progeny their guardians and helpers while forsaking God, a wretched choice of substitute.
rows.anchor: they have made them their real guardians and helpers, and forsaken God. Then while turning away from them it is stated that how evil a substitute they have adopted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab idolaters worshipped jinn to ward off harm, treated mountains and valleys as a jinn’s domain, and sacrificed children because they feared an unsacrificed child would be consumed by the jinn.
rows.anchor: They thought that if one of the children was not sacrificed to please one of the jinn, he would consume all of them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’ān appeals to Quraysh’s honor: they follow Iblīs, a jinn who showed enmity toward their ancestor Adam.
rows.anchor: Iblīs was from amog the jinn. They have become his disciples in spite of the fact that Ibīs had shown such enmity for Adam (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Wrongdoers’ means idolaters; the phrase about an evil substitute expresses sorrow and wonder that they replaced God with the eternal enemy of their forefather and his descendants.
rows.anchor: expresses sorrow and wonder: if these wrongdoers found a substitute for God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s sarcasm points out that God neither consulted devils about creation nor appointed misleaders as helpers, although the idolaters treat them as divine associates.
rows.anchor: The style of this verse is sarcastic: these people have so generously made these devils associates of God even though He never called them for help

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse recalls the idolaters’ deprivation on Judgment Day, when a pit of destruction separates them from the idols they invoked.
rows.anchor: This verse reminds them of their deprivation on that day. The pit of destruction will obstruct the idolaters and their idols from one another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wrongdoers will see their destruction approaching and be helpless to escape it.
rows.anchor: The verse expresses the state of helplessness of the wrongdoers: they will have knowledge of their destruction and fall into it while seeing their fate.
